doc.title: Gerald Wiggins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 2, 1995

title: Road stories and the Armstrong southern tour
summary: Fifty one-nighters through the segregated South with Armstrong led him to quit, and a surprise Georgia stop with Benny Carter.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you have any road stories that you can share with us?
I can’t tell them, no. I can’t even write a book about them.
They don’t translate on to film, huh?
Well, my lips are sealed, believe me.
How about the best road experience you had, either with Les Hite or anybody from—

Well I had fun with all the gigs I had, with the singers and the bands, you know. There were good times and bad times. I think the worst time I had was when I joined Louis Armstrong. I joined Louis out here, and we made 50 one nighters, all through the south. And at that time the south was pretty bad. So two weeks before we got to New York, I put in my notice. I loved the band and everything but I just couldn’t stand what we were going through. It wasn’t very nice. Anyhow we got to New York and I was home about three or four days and Benny Carter called me. He says, “Wig, you want to go take a trip to the west coast?” I said, “Yeah.” I said, “You’re not going south are you?” He said, “Oh, no, don’t even think about that.” I got on the train with Bumps Myers and I went to sleep and I woke up and I was in Macon, Georgia. I’d like to die. I gave him my notice right then and there. And he said, “Okay.” And that was the end of it. And J.J. Johnson and Max Roach they say, “Oh Wig, come on” you know. So a couple of days later I went to Benny and I said, “About that notice I gave you I’d like to take it back.” He said, “What notice?” I said, “Oh, okay.”
Was there a difference in that tour than with Louis?
Well we didn’t stay there. Benny wasn’t about to stay down there.
Louis went down in the south quite a bit, didn’t he?
Well that was his territory. It sure wasn’t mine.
What was it like musically working with him?

Well I never knew because with Louis we just played a gig and get out of town. We really didn’t have a chance to meet anybody. By the time you got there it was time to play. When you finished you packed up and on to the next town. We were making like 500 mile jumps every night. So it was a little rough.
